lessons.title: Le réveil du printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe and document spring changes in their environment

mindsOn.activity: Circle time with spring awakening sounds. Play recordings of birds, rain, wind through leaves. Ask 'Qu'est-ce que c'est?' Show spring vocabulary cards with actions: PRINTEMPS (stretch like growing plant), NATURE (open arms wide), OBSERVER (binocular hands).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Large seasonal pictures showing winter to spring transition, vocabulary cards with nature symbols
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students are sleepy: Add more movement with growing plant stretches. If they're excited about sounds: Extend sound identification and let them make nature sounds.

activities: Spring Detective Walk (~10 min): Walk outside or to windows. Look for spring signs: new leaves, flowers, animals. Point saying 'Je vois le printemps!' Students copy gesture and repeat. Record findings on clipboards with simple drawings.

Observation Journals (~10 min): Each student gets simple journal page with spring date. Draw or write (with help) three spring things they observed. Use vocabulary: 'J'observe...' and point to drawings.

Spring Changes Discussion (~7 min): Compare winter photos to current observations. Use gestures for 'avant' (yesterday gesture) and 'maintenant' (now gesture). Students say 'Maintenant c'est le printemps!'
action.visualSupport: Photos of same locations in winter vs spring, simple drawing templates for observations
action.decisionPoint: If weather prevents outside: Use classroom window observations or indoor plants, extend with spring picture books. If students finish quickly: Let them add color to their journal drawings.

consolidation.activity: Spring Gallery Walk. Post observation journals around room. Students walk quietly, looking at each other's spring discoveries. End with group celebration: everyone points outside and shouts 'Bonjour printemps!'
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify spring elements when asked 'Où est le printemps?' Do they use observation gestures with 'observer'? Can they share one thing they noticed about spring?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students are very engaged with sharing: Allow more time for individual sharing about their drawings. If energy is low: Skip gallery walk and do seated sharing in circle.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Indoor spring exploration: Use houseplants, spring picture books, or videos of spring scenes. Students can practice vocabulary while pointing to spring elements in pictures.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Noticing buds on trees, new flowers, changing weather, animals returning - encourage daily spring observation walks with family

lessons.title: Collection de trésors naturels
lessons.oneGoal: Students will ethically collect natural materials for art-making

mindsOn.activity: Review spring vocabulary from Lesson 1 with actions. Introduce collecting vocabulary: RAMASSER (picking up gesture), FEUILLE (hold up leaf shape with hands), FLEUR (cup hands like flower). Practice 'gentle touch' - soft fingers for handling nature.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Real examples of leaves and flowers, collection baskets, pictures showing gentle vs rough handling
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students want to grab immediately: Practice 'gentle fingers' more with feathers or soft fabric. If they're cautious: Model enthusiastic but careful collecting.

activities: Nature Collection Rules (~5 min): Learn 'take only what has fallen' rule. Practice saying 'Je ramasse doucement.' Show picking up fallen leaves vs leaving flowers growing. Use thumbs up for good choices.

Treasure Hunt Collection (~15 min): Go outside with small baskets. Look for: fallen leaves, interesting twigs, smooth stones, empty shells. Say vocabulary as you find: 'Une feuille!' Count treasures: 'Un, deux, trois!'
Sorting and Organizing (~7 min): Back inside, sort treasures by type, color, or size. Create display on table. Practice describing: 'Ma feuille est rouge.' 'Mon bâton est long.'
action.visualSupport: Visual rules poster with pictures, color-coded sorting areas, size comparison examples
action.decisionPoint: If students collect too much: Set gentle limits like '5 treasures each.' If they can't find enough: Expand search area or provide backup natural materials.

consolidation.activity: Treasure Museum. Each student chooses their favorite treasure to share. Hold it up saying 'Mon trésor spécial!' Others respond 'Merci, nature!' Practice vocabulary by describing color, size, or texture of special treasure.
consolidation.assessment: Can students collect gently without breaking living plants? Do they use 'ramasser' with appropriate gesture? Can they identify 'feuille' and 'fleur' in their collection?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students are proud of collections: Allow extra time for detailed sharing and compliments. If they're tired from outdoor time: Do quiet seated sharing with whispering voices.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Pre-collected nature materials: Use teacher collection of safe natural items. Students can still practice gentle handling, sorting, and vocabulary with provided materials.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Finding interesting leaves, stones, twigs in their yard or neighborhood - remind them of gentle collection rules at home

lessons.title: Art éphémère dehors
lessons.oneGoal: Students will create temporary art installations outdoors

mindsOn.activity: Introduce 'temporaire' concept: Build a simple block tower, then gently knock it down. Say 'Art temporaire!' Show pictures of sand castles, chalk art, snow sculptures that don't last forever. Practice vocabulary with gestures.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Photos of ephemeral art (sand castles, chalk art, ice sculptures), blocks for demonstration
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students seem upset about temporary art: Emphasize the fun of creating and taking photos to remember. If they understand quickly: Show more complex ephemeral art examples.

activities: Outdoor Art Spaces (~5 min): Go outside and find good spots for temporary art: flat ground, tree bases, sandbox areas. Practice saying 'Ici, dehors!' and 'Mon espace d'art!'

Natural Mandala Creation (~15 min): Using collected materials from Lesson 2, create circular patterns on ground. Start with center piece, work outward. Say 'arrangement' as you place each item. No glue or permanent attachment.
Photography Documentation (~7 min): Take simple photos of creations with tablets/cameras. Practice saying 'Ma photo!' Then gently return materials to nature, saying 'Au revoir, art!'
action.visualSupport: Examples of simple mandala patterns, demonstration of center-to-outside arrangement
action.decisionPoint: If weather is poor: Create temporary arrangements indoors on large paper, emphasizing that paper will be recycled. If students struggle with circular patterns: Allow free-form arrangements.

consolidation.activity: Photo Gallery Review. Look at photos taken of everyone's temporary art. Practice vocabulary: 'Mon art temporaire était dehors!' Celebrate the beauty of creating art that doesn't need to last forever.
consolidation.assessment: Can students explain 'temporaire' concept in their own words? Do they create arrangements using natural materials? Are they comfortable with art that doesn't permanently last?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students love their photos: Print them immediately for take-home if possible. If they seem sad about temporary nature: emphasize the joy and memory of creating.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Indoor temporary art: Use natural materials to create arrangements on large paper sheets that will later be recycled, emphasizing the temporary nature.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Making patterns with sidewalk chalk that rain will wash away, building sandcastles that waves take away

lessons.title: Land art miniature
lessons.oneGoal: Students will create small-scale land art using natural materials

mindsOn.activity: Show examples of large land art (photos) vs small land art they'll make. Practice vocabulary: PETIT (pinch fingers close), CERCLE (draw circle in air), SPIRALE (spiral finger motion from center out). Use arms for big, fingers for small.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Photos of famous land art, small examples made by teacher, finger/hand gesture cards
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students fascinated by big land art photos: Spend more time discussing what they see. If they want to start immediately: Move quickly to demonstration of small-scale work.

activities: Pattern Practice (~8 min): Using indoor materials (blocks, buttons), practice making small circles and spirals on desks. Say patterns as you make them: 'petit cercle,' 'spirale.' Take turns being pattern directors.
Outdoor Mini Land Art (~15 min): Find small outdoor spaces (1 foot square). Create tiny land art using pebbles, leaves, twigs. Work individually or in pairs. Practice vocabulary: 'Mon petit art!'
Mini Gallery Walk (~4 min): Visit each other's small creations. Use quiet voices outdoors. Give compliments: 'J'aime ta spirale!' Take photos if desired.
materials: Small natural materials sorted by type
action.visualSupport: Viewfinder frames to help students define their small workspace, pattern example cards
action.decisionPoint: If students make very large art: Gently redirect with viewfinder frames to show 'petit' concept. If they finish quickly: Let them create second mini artwork nearby.

consolidation.activity: Scale Comparison. Compare their mini land art to photos of large land art. Discuss: 'Grand ou petit?' Practice size vocabulary. Celebrate that small art can be just as beautiful and meaningful as large art.
consolidation.assessment: Can students work within small scale boundaries? Do they create intentional patterns with 'cercle' or 'spirale'? Can they use 'petit' appropriately to describe their work?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to preserve their work: Take detailed photos and discuss why outdoor art is temporary. If they're ready for bigger scale: Promise future lessons with larger projects.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Tabletop land art: Use natural materials on individual desk spaces, emphasizing small scale and pattern-making vocabulary.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Arranging shells at the beach, making fairy circles with acorns, creating small rock arrangements in gardens

lessons.title: Couleurs de printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will match and recreate spring colors in their art

mindsOn.activity: Spring color hunt in classroom. Look around and identify spring colors already present. Practice vocabulary: VERT (point to green items), ROSE (point to pink items), VIOLET (point to purple items). Use color cards to match what students find.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Large color cards in spring shades, real spring items (flowers, leaves) in target colors
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If classroom lacks spring colors: Use picture books or spring photos to identify colors. If students know these colors well: Introduce color mixing concepts.

activities: Nature Color Matching (~10 min): Go outside with color cards. Find natural items that match 'vert,' 'rose,' 'violet.' Hold up card next to natural item saying 'C'est vert!' Collect small samples if appropriate.
Spring Color Mixing (~12 min): Using paints or natural materials (crushed flowers, grass stains), try to recreate spring colors. Mix different greens, pinks, purples. Say 'Je mélange' while mixing.
Color Pattern Art (~5 min): Create simple patterns using spring colors: green-pink-green-pink or purple-green-purple-green. Use painted papers or natural materials arranged by color.
materials: Color matching cards in spring shades
action.visualSupport: Color mixing chart showing how to make spring colors, pattern examples
action.decisionPoint: If mixing is too messy: Use pre-mixed spring colors for pattern making. If students love mixing: Allow more time for color experimentation.

consolidation.activity: Spring Color Gallery. Display color mixing results and patterns. Students walk around identifying colors: 'Je vois du vert!' Vote on 'most spring-like color' creation. Sing simple color song using spring vocabulary.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify 'vert,' 'rose,' and 'violet' in nature? Do they attempt to match colors from environment? Can they create intentional color patterns?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students are very engaged with color mixing: Plan follow-up color exploration activities. If they prefer natural materials: Focus more on arranging found items by color.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Indoor spring color exploration: Use magazines, colored paper, or picture books to identify and sort spring colors by vocabulary words.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Noticing new green grass, pink blossoms, purple crocuses on walks with family - creating a home color collection

lessons.title: Textures naturelles
lessons.oneGoal: Students will explore and recreate natural textures in their artwork

mindsOn.activity: Texture mystery box: Students feel different natural textures (bark, smooth stone, soft moss) without looking. Describe what they feel. Introduce vocabulary: TEXTURE (run fingers across palm), RUGUEUX (rough scratching motion), LISSE (smooth stroking motion).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Texture vocabulary cards with tactile examples glued on, collection of natural items with obvious different textures
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students struggle with texture vocabulary: Focus on just 'rugueux' and 'lisse' with clear examples. If they understand quickly: Add more texture words like 'doux' (soft).

activities: Outdoor Texture Hunt (~10 min): Walk outside touching different natural surfaces safely. Tree bark, smooth rocks, grass, flower petals. Say texture vocabulary as you feel: 'C'est rugueux!' 'C'est lisse!'

Texture Rubbings (~12 min): Place paper over textured natural surfaces (bark, leaves, rocks). Rub with crayons to capture texture. Say 'Je frotte pour la texture!' Compare rubbings to actual textures.
Texture Collage (~5 min): Arrange texture rubbings by type: all rough textures together, all smooth textures together. Practice vocabulary while organizing.
materials: Collection bags for safe texture samples
action.visualSupport: Demonstration of proper rubbing technique, texture sorting mats labeled with vocabulary
action.decisionPoint: If rubbings don't work well: Focus on direct touching and vocabulary practice. If students love texture exploration: Allow time to create texture maps of playground areas.

consolidation.activity: Texture Museum. Display texture rubbings and samples. Students touch and identify: 'Cette texture est rugueuse!' Visitors (other students) can feel and guess textures. End with texture vocabulary song.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify 'rugueux' and 'lisse' by touch? Do they use texture vocabulary while exploring? Can they successfully create texture rubbings?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to continue exploring: Set up texture exploration station for free choice time. If they're overwhelmed by choices: Focus on just 2-3 very different textures.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Indoor texture exploration: Use classroom materials (sandpaper, fabric, plastic) and houseplants to practice texture vocabulary and create rubbings.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Feeling tree bark, smooth stones, soft moss, prickly pine cones - creating texture collections at home

lessons.title: Empreintes de nature
lessons.oneGoal: Students will make prints and rubbings from natural objects

mindsOn.activity: Show handprints and footprints as examples of 'empreintes.' Press hands in playdough, then lift to show print left behind. Introduce vocabulary: EMPREINTE (press hand then lift), FROTTER (rubbing motion), PAPIER (hold up paper sheets).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Examples of animal tracks, leaf prints, handprints in different materials
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students want to make many handprints: Set time limit but let them enjoy the concept. If they understand prints quickly: Move to natural object printing.

activities: Nature Print Setup (~5 min): Prepare printing stations with paint pads, paper, natural objects (leaves, flowers, bark pieces). Demonstrate: dip object in paint, press on paper, lift carefully saying 'Mon empreinte!'

Print Exploration (~15 min): Students try printing with different natural objects. Compare prints to original objects. Layer different prints on same paper. Practice vocabulary: 'Je frotte' for rubbings, 'J'imprime' for paint prints.
Print Comparison (~7 min): Compare today's prints to texture rubbings from Lesson 6. Which method shows texture better? Which shows shape better? Sort prints by technique used.
materials: Paint pads or shallow paint dishes
action.visualSupport: Step-by-step printing demonstration cards, examples of successful prints
action.decisionPoint: If printing is too messy: Switch to dry methods like pencil rubbings. If students love printing: Allow multiple colors and layered prints.

consolidation.activity: Print Gallery and Detective Game. Display prints around room. Students try to guess which natural object made each print. Point to print saying 'Cette empreinte vient de...' Celebrate successful detective work.
consolidation.assessment: Can students create clear prints using natural objects? Do they understand 'empreinte' concept? Can they use 'frotter' and related vocabulary appropriately?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students struggle with detective game: Focus on their own prints and describing process. If they excel at guessing: Create more challenging prints with less obvious objects.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Classroom object printing: Use textured classroom materials (sponges, textured blocks, stamps) to practice printing vocabulary and techniques.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Making leaf rubbings like they might do on nature walks with family, noticing animal tracks in mud or sand

lessons.title: Jardin artistique
lessons.oneGoal: Students will design and create a small artistic garden space

mindsOn.activity: Show pictures of different gardens: vegetable gardens, flower gardens, artistic gardens with patterns. Discuss what makes a garden 'artistic.' Introduce vocabulary: JARDIN (sweeping arm gesture), PLANTER (digging and placing motion), GRANDIR (start small, grow tall with arms).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Photos of artistic gardens, regular gardens, and wild nature areas for comparison
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students have limited garden experience: Focus on container gardens and indoor plants. If they're very knowledgeable: Let them share garden experiences and knowledge.

activities: Garden Design Planning (~8 min): On paper, draw simple garden design. Choose colors, shapes, patterns for plant arrangement. Think artistically: 'Comment mon jardin sera beau?' Use circles for flowers, lines for rows.

Mini Garden Creation (~15 min): Using small containers, plant seeds or small plants in artistic arrangements. Create patterns with different plants. Say 'Je plante artistiquement!' Focus on beauty, not just growth.
Garden Care Instructions (~4 min): Discuss how plants will 'grandir.' Plan care schedule. Practice saying 'Mon jardin va grandir!' Make simple care reminder cards with pictures.
action.visualSupport: Garden design templates, examples of artistic plant arrangements, plant care pictorial instructions
action.decisionPoint: If no outdoor space available: Focus on container gardens that can stay indoors. If students struggle with design: Provide simple templates to follow.

consolidation.activity: Garden Gallery. Display mini gardens and design plans. Students explain their artistic choices: 'J'ai planté comme ça parce que...' Set up observation schedule to watch gardens grow over coming weeks.
consolidation.assessment: Can students explain their artistic garden choices? Do they understand that plants will 'grandir'? Can they use garden vocabulary appropriately?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If gardens need immediate care: Set up watering schedule right away. If students are very excited about growth: Plan regular observation and documentation activities.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Paper garden art: Create artistic garden designs using colored paper, stickers, or drawings, discussing how real gardens could be designed artistically.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Helping with family garden, choosing flowers for beauty and growth, creating mini gardens at home

lessons.title: Mobile de printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will create hanging mobiles using collected natural materials

mindsOn.activity: Demonstrate balance with simple balance scale or seesaw motion with arms. Show mobile examples moving in air currents. Introduce vocabulary: SUSPENDU (hang finger from other finger), ÉQUILIBRE (balance arms like scale), MOUVEMENT (gentle swaying motion).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Simple balance scale, examples of mobiles in motion, vocabulary cards with gesture demonstrations
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students struggle with balance concept: Use more concrete examples like balance scales. If they understand quickly: Show complex mobiles with multiple balance points.

activities: Balance Experiments (~8 min): Using sticks and natural materials, experiment with balance. Place items on either end of stick held in middle. Find balance point. Say 'Équilibre!' when balanced, adjust when needed.

Mobile Assembly (~15 min): Using balanced sticks, string, and natural materials from previous lessons, assemble simple mobiles. Start with one balanced stick, add hanging elements. Test movement by gently blowing.
Movement Testing (~4 min): Hang mobiles in areas with gentle air movement (near fan, open door). Observe movement. Practice vocabulary: 'Mon mobile est suspendu et il bouge!'
materials: Collected natural materials from previous lessons
action.visualSupport: Step-by-step mobile assembly pictures, examples of balanced and unbalanced arrangements
action.decisionPoint: If balance is too difficult: Pre-balance some elements and focus on hanging and movement. If students excel: Let them create multi-level mobiles with several balance points.

consolidation.activity: Mobile Exhibition. Hang all mobiles in classroom where they can move freely. Students observe each other's work, describing what they see: 'Ce mobile a du mouvement!' Test different ways to create gentle movement.
consolidation.assessment: Can students create balanced arrangements? Do they understand 'suspendu' and 'mouvement' concepts? Can they adjust their mobile when it's unbalanced?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If mobiles break easily: Focus on appreciation and gentle handling. If they're very successful: Plan to hang them permanently in classroom or take home.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Paper mobiles: Create mobiles using paper cutouts of natural shapes, focusing on balance and movement concepts without fragile natural materials.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Wind chimes on porches, things hanging from trees in wind, watching leaves and flowers move in breeze

lessons.title: Photographie nature
lessons.oneGoal: Students will document nature art through simple photography techniques

mindsOn.activity: Look at photos of nature art from previous lessons. Discuss what makes a good photo vs bad photo. Introduce vocabulary: PHOTOGRAPHIER (camera holding gesture), ANGLE (tilt head/hands different ways), LUMIÈRE (point to light sources).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Examples of same subject photographed from different angles and lighting, simple cameras or tablets
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students have limited camera experience: Focus on holding device steady and pressing button. If they're experienced: Discuss composition and interesting angles.

activities: Photography Practice (~8 min): Using classroom objects, practice taking photos from different angles. High, low, close, far. Compare results. Practice vocabulary: 'Je photographie d'un angle différent!'

Nature Art Documentation (~15 min): Go outside and photograph previous nature art creations or create new temporary art to photograph. Try different angles and lighting. Take multiple photos of same subject.
Photo Review and Selection (~4 min): Look at photos taken. Choose favorites. Discuss why some photos are more interesting: 'Cette photo a une bonne lumière!' 'Cet angle est intéressant!'
materials: Previously created nature art or materials for new art
action.visualSupport: Examples of good vs poor photography composition, angle demonstration cards
action.decisionPoint: If technology isn't working: Focus on discussing photography concepts and planning shots without taking them. If photos are excellent: Plan to create class photo book.

consolidation.activity: Photography Exhibition Planning. Choose best photos for class exhibition. Practice describing photos using vocabulary: 'J'ai photographié avec cette lumière...' Plan how to share photos with families.
consolidation.assessment: Can students hold camera steady and take focused photos? Do they experiment with different angles? Can they identify good lighting in their photos?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If photos need editing: Keep editing very simple or skip it. If students want to continue: Plan regular photography documentation of nature changes.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Photography planning: Without cameras, use viewfinder frames to 'frame' shots and discuss angles and lighting, planning future photography sessions.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Taking pictures of their gardens, pets, special places outdoors - sharing nature photos with family

lessons.title: Art avec les saisons
lessons.oneGoal: Students will plan art projects that change with seasonal cycles

mindsOn.activity: Review four seasons with pictures and actions. Discuss how nature changes through seasons. Introduce vocabulary: CYCLE (circular motion with arms), CHANGEMENT (transform gestures from one thing to another), SAISON (hold up 4 fingers, name each season).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Four seasons picture cards, circular diagram showing seasonal cycle, transformation examples
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students struggle with seasonal concept: Focus on just current season vs one other season. If they understand well: Discuss specific changes they've noticed.

activities: Seasonal Art Planning (~10 min): Choose one outdoor location (tree, garden bed, etc.). Plan different art projects for each season using that same location. Draw simple plans: spring flowers, summer leaves, fall colors, winter shapes.
Long-term Project Start (~10 min): Begin a season-tracking project. Could be: seasonal photo series, seasonal collection display, seasonal art in same location. Document current spring state.
Future Season Predictions (~7 min): Discuss and draw predictions: 'En été, cet arbre aura...' 'En automne, cette fleur sera...' Practice vocabulary while predicting changes.
materials: Art materials for current season documentation
action.visualSupport: Seasonal cycle diagram, examples of same locations in different seasons, planning templates
action.decisionPoint: If planning is too abstract: Focus on documenting current season thoroughly. If students are very engaged: Help them set up detailed long-term observation projects.

consolidation.activity: Seasonal Art Calendar. Create simple calendar marking when to check seasonal art projects. Practice vocabulary: 'Le cycle des saisons change mon art!' Set reminders for future observations.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify seasonal cycles? Do they understand that nature and art will change over time? Can they make reasonable predictions about seasonal changes?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students are confused by long-term planning: Focus on immediate seasonal observations. If they're excited about tracking: Help them create detailed observation schedules.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Seasonal art comparison: Use photos and examples to compare how the same art project would look different in each season, discussing vocabulary without long-term planning.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Watching their planted gardens grow, trees change through year, creating seasonal decorations at home

lessons.title: Installation collaborative
lessons.oneGoal: Students will work together to create a large environmental art installation

mindsOn.activity: Review smaller art projects from previous lessons. Discuss working together: what works well, what's challenging. Introduce vocabulary: ENSEMBLE (link arms with classmates), GRAND (stretch arms wide), COLLABORATION (shake hands, work together gestures).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Photos of large-scale collaborative art projects, examples of teamwork in art-making
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students have collaboration challenges: Practice simple cooperative activities first. If they work well together: Jump into complex installation planning.

activities: Installation Planning (~8 min): As a class, choose location and theme for large environmental art installation. Everyone contributes ideas. Vote on final design. Practice: 'Nous travaillons ensemble!' Plan individual roles.

Collaborative Creation (~15 min): Work together on installation. Some students collect materials, others arrange, others document. Rotate roles. Use vocabulary: 'Notre grand art!' 'Collaboration artistique!'
Installation Completion (~4 min): Step back and admire completed work. Each student shares one thing they contributed: 'J'ai ajouté...' Photograph final installation from multiple angles.
materials: Tools for arrangement (rakes, shovels if needed)
action.visualSupport: Examples of successful collaborative installations, role assignment cards, teamwork reminder posters
action.decisionPoint: If collaboration breaks down: Assign specific roles and smaller groups. If working smoothly: Allow creative expansion of original plan.

consolidation.activity: Installation Celebration. Gather around completed installation. Each student says one word describing the collaboration: 'Magnifique!' 'Ensemble!' 'Grand!' Plan how to share installation with school community.
consolidation.assessment: Can students work effectively in large group? Do they contribute to collaborative decisions? Can they use collaboration vocabulary appropriately?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If installation is very successful: Plan regular community viewing times. If it needs work: Focus on celebrating effort and teamwork over final product.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Classroom collaborative installation: Create large-scale art installation indoors using collected natural materials, focusing on teamwork and vocabulary.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Working with neighbors on community gardens, school beautification projects, family art projects

lessons.title: Respect pour l'environnement
lessons.oneGoal: Students will demonstrate understanding of environmental responsibility in art

mindsOn.activity: Discuss how they've used nature in their art. What happened to natural materials? What stayed in nature? Introduce vocabulary: RESPECTER (gentle handling gesture), PROTÉGER (sheltering arms), RESPONSABLE (point to self, responsible gesture).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Before/after photos of art-making locations, examples of responsible vs irresponsible nature use
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students seem confused about environmental impact: Use concrete examples from their own art-making. If they're environmentally aware: Discuss more complex conservation concepts.

activities: Environmental Audit (~10 min): Visit locations where class made environmental art. Check impact: are locations healthier, same, or damaged? Discuss observations. Practice: 'Nous respectons la nature.'

Responsibility Guidelines (~10 min): Create class rules for environmental art. Decide: what materials can we take? What should we never disturb? How to leave areas better than we found them? Post guidelines.

Restoration Project (~7 min): Choose one area that needs care. Clean up litter, replant disturbed areas, or improve habitat. Practice vocabulary: 'Nous protégeons notre environnement!' 'C'est notre responsabilité!'
materials: Materials for minor restoration (seeds, small plants, cleanup supplies)
action.visualSupport: Environmental impact comparison photos, restoration example pictures, responsibility checklist
action.decisionPoint: If students find environmental damage: Use it as learning opportunity without blame. If everything looks good: focus on maintaining good practices.

consolidation.activity: Environmental Promise. Students make personal promises about how they'll be responsible environmental artists. Share promises: 'Je promets de respecter...' Create display of class environmental art guidelines.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify environmental responsibility concepts? Do they understand impact of art-making on nature? Can they use responsibility vocabulary meaningfully?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students make unrealistic promises: Help them create achievable goals. If they're very committed: Help them plan ongoing environmental action.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Environmental art ethics discussion: Use photos and scenarios to discuss responsible environmental art practices without outdoor assessment.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Leaving nature spaces better than they found them, teaching family members about environmental responsibility

lessons.title: Art et météo
lessons.oneGoal: Students will create art that responds to or incorporates weather conditions

mindsOn.activity: Check current weather conditions. Act out different weather: PLUIE (finger rain), SOLEIL (arms in circle overhead), VENT (swaying motion). Discuss how weather affects outdoor art. What art works in each weather?
mindsOn.visualSupport: Weather cards with symbols and actions, examples of weather-responsive art
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If weather is severe: Plan indoor weather art simulation. If weather is perfect: Take full advantage for outdoor weather art creation.

activities: Weather Art Planning (~7 min): Based on current weather, plan appropriate art. Rainy day: water art, puddle art. Sunny day: shadow art, sun-dried art. Windy day: movement art, wind-powered art.
Weather-Responsive Creation (~15 min): Create art that uses current weather conditions. Let rain add to art, use sun to dry or warm materials, let wind move elements. Say: 'Le météo aide mon art!'
Weather Adaptation (~5 min): If weather changes during creation, adapt art accordingly. Practice problem-solving: 'Maintenant il pleut, alors je...' Embrace weather as art collaborator.
materials: Weather-appropriate art materials (water-soluble paints for rain, light materials for wind, etc.)
action.visualSupport: Weather-art matching cards, examples of successful weather adaptations
action.decisionPoint: If weather makes art impossible: Focus on planning and small-scale weather simulation indoors. If weather is too changeable: Create art that works in multiple weather conditions.

consolidation.activity: Weather Art Documentation. Photograph art with weather conditions visible. Discuss how weather helped or challenged art-making. Practice vocabulary: 'Avec la pluie, mon art...' Plan weather art for different seasons.
consolidation.assessment: Can students adapt their art to weather conditions? Do they use weather vocabulary appropriately? Can they see weather as artistic opportunity rather than obstacle?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students struggled with weather adaptation: Plan more weather simulation activities. If they loved weather art: create weather art stations for different conditions.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Indoor weather art: Simulate weather conditions indoors (spray bottles for rain, fans for wind, lamps for sun) and practice weather vocabulary with art-making.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Puddle jumping, shadow play, flying kites, catching snowflakes - weather as natural art partner

lessons.title: Expo nature printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will curate and present their environmental art collection

mindsOn.activity: Review all environmental art created during unit. Look at photos, saved examples, documentation. Discuss what exhibition means. Introduce vocabulary: EXPOSITION (gesture showing display), PRÉSENTER (formal showing gesture), PARTAGER (giving/sharing motion).
mindsOn.visualSupport: Photos of previous art projects from unit, examples of art exhibitions, vocabulary cards for presentation
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students have forgotten earlier projects: Spend more time reviewing and reconnecting with their work. If they remember well: Focus on selection and presentation planning.

activities: Exhibition Curation (~10 min): Choose best examples from unit for exhibition. Consider: variety, growth shown, personal favorites. Practice vocabulary: 'Je choisis cette œuvre pour l'exposition parce que...'
Presentation Preparation (~12 min): Prepare to present chosen works. Write or practice simple descriptions in French. Arrange display. Create labels with key vocabulary from lessons.
Exhibition Setup (~5 min): Set up formal exhibition space. Arrange work thoughtfully. Practice walking through as visitors. Make final adjustments: 'Notre exposition est prête!'
materials: All documentation and preserved work from unit
action.visualSupport: Exhibition layout examples, label templates, presentation planning sheets
action.decisionPoint: If students struggle with selection: Help them choose representative samples from each lesson. If they want to include everything: discuss curation concepts.

consolidation.activity: Exhibition Opening. Invite other classes or family members if possible. Students present their work: 'Voici mon art environnemental!' Practice vocabulary while sharing. Celebrate growth and learning throughout unit.
consolidation.assessment: Can students select and present their work thoughtfully? Do they use unit vocabulary appropriately in presentations? Can they share their environmental art learning with others?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If no visitors available: Students present to each other in formal exhibition format. If many visitors: organize into small presentation groups.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Virtual exhibition: Create digital exhibition using photos and recordings of student presentations, focusing on vocabulary use and reflection.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Sharing nature discoveries with family, creating outdoor displays at home, continuing environmental art exploration

beginningSpeaker.description: Student uses 1-2 vocabulary words with support, participates in activities with guidance, creates simple environmental art with help
indicators: Creates basic nature art with assistance

developingSpeaker.description: Student uses 3-5 vocabulary words independently, participates actively in most activities, creates environmental art with some independence
indicators: Creates art that shows environmental awareness

expandingSpeaker.description: Student uses 6+ vocabulary words in sentences, leads some activities, creates complex environmental art independently

bridgingSpeaker.description: Student uses extensive vocabulary naturally, teaches others, creates sophisticated environmental art and explains process
indicators: Creates and explains complex environmental art
